title: The Real World Is Not a Dropdown Menu: Why Fixed-Label Vision Models Break Down
summary: Why fixed-label vision models break down in the open world, and how CLIP-style zero-shot learning and modern VLMs change the interface.
body_text: A Simple Assumption With Big Limits Computer vision has seen tremendous progress in the last decade. Vision models can perform tasks such as image classification, object detection, pixel-level segmentation, and visual retrieval. In the right domain, today’s systems can provide very strong results. But many traditional visual recognition systems operate under a simple constraint: they recognize visual data using a fixed set of predefined categories. This approach works well for constrained tasks. A model trained on digits only has to distinguish between ten possible digits. Similarly, a model trained on cats, dogs, cars, and airplanes only has to choose between those four categories. However, this approach fails to capture many open-ended applications, where the model has to reason about a wide range of concepts. Fixed-label systems become limiting when a task requires: Understanding or describing objects that the model has not seen before. Describing rare or anomalous phenomena. Matching a visual observation against a description, such as “the image shows X.” Answering unusual questions that the model was not trained on. The Fixed-Label Era Traditional image classification systems are often built on the following setup: acquire and curate a labeled dataset, train a vision model to recognize images as belonging to a fixed set of labels, and use that model to perform classification. Two major types of models used for these computer vision systems are Convolutional Neural Networks, or CNNs, and Vision Transformers, or ViTs. Both can be used for vision classification tasks, with CNNs learning hierarchical patterns in images through learned convolutional filters and ViTs dividing images into patches before analyzing context with self-attention. Image → CNN / ViT → fixed class label prediction A traditional CNN classifier extracts visual features from an image, passes them through a classifier, and outputs probabilities over a fixed set of classes. Source: adapted from IONOS Digital Guide. The main limitation is not the architecture itself. It is the fixed set of output labels. While CNNs and ViTs can learn rich visual patterns, many supervised classification systems are still constrained to differentiate between a fixed set of classes. Where Fixed Labels Fail Open-ended environments, however, contain tasks that go beyond distinguishing between a handful of classes. The real world often contains new objects, rare corner cases, and anomalous observations that may not be represented by a system’s predefined categories or task-specific training data. It also contains questions and descriptions that a vision system was not explicitly trained to answer. For example, a robot may need to follow an instruction like “pick up the red cup next to the laptop,” which requires reasoning about objects, attributes, and spatial relationships rather than choosing from a single fixed category. Similarly, a manufacturing application might require a model to analyze defects. A binary “good” or “bad” label may not be sufficient to describe the type, location, or severity of the defect. What Real-World Vision Systems Need More flexible vision systems need to perform open-ended reasoning to answer questions such as: What is happening here? How should this scene be described? What changed from the last image to this image? Does this image depict X or not? Does this image provide evidence for claim X? This requires systems that move from a closed set of possible answers, such as class labels, to more flexible answers that are grounded in what the image shows. Traditional image classification tasks have a fixed set of answers. Newer tasks move toward more open-ended outputs, such as captions, descriptions, retrieval results, or natural language answers. This changes the interface from one where the user asks “what is this image?” and the system answers with a label, to one where the user asks “does this image depict X?” and the system answers using natural language. One way to relax this constraint is through zero-shot or few-shot methods. These approaches allow models to recognize or adapt to concepts without requiring a large task-specific labeled dataset, using broader sources of supervision such as natural language or a small number of examples. Zero-Shot Image Classification Using Natural Language Supervision CLIP, or Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training, uses a large-scale dataset of 400 million image-text pairs collected from the internet. The model uses an image encoder and a text encoder, both projecting their outputs into a shared embedding space (Radford et al., 2021). CLIP learns a shared embedding space for images and text by contrastively training image and text encoders to align matching pairs and separate mismatched pairs. Source: OpenAI. During training, for every batch of image-text pairs, the model compares image and text embeddings using cosine similarity. It learns to bring the embeddings of correct image-text pairs closer together while pushing apart the embeddings of incorrect image-text pairs (Radford et al., 2021). Essentially, the model learns associations between visual concepts and language without being explicitly trained for one specific computer vision task. A key property of CLIP is that it can perform zero-shot classification. Given an image, the model can compare natural language prompt options and select the one that is the best match. One can use prompts such as “a photo of a cat” or “a photo of a dog” as candidate descriptions and select the one with the highest cosine similarity to the image embedding. Zero-shot learning allows a model to classify an unseen category by using semantic information, such as attributes or natural language descriptions, rather than relying only on examples of that exact class. Source: ModulAI. The candidate classes do not need to be encoded in a task-specific classification head. Instead, class labels can be provided as natural language prompts to the text encoder. It is important to note that the usefulness of such approaches is highly contextual and depends on the exact task, prompt design, and distance of test examples from the training distribution. Nevertheless, such methods provide a valuable shift from fixed output classes toward matching images with flexible natural-language descriptions. From CLIP to Modern VLMs While CLIP is a powerful tool for zero-shot image classification and image-text retrieval, it is not a fully fledged vision-language assistant. Given an image, CLIP does not directly generate free-form natural language captions or answers. Modern vision-language models, or VLMs, extend this approach by generating language from visual input. One approach, used by LLaVA (Liu et al., 2023), is to connect a vision encoder with a large language model using a projection layer. The vision encoder generates embeddings of the input image, and the projection layer, usually a single linear layer or sometimes a small neural network, maps these embeddings into a space the language model can process alongside text tokens. Another approach, used by Flamingo (Alayrac et al., 2022), connects vision and language through cross-attention layers. The general idea behind these models is to allow the language model to use visual information while performing downstream tasks such as captioning, visual question answering, and multimodal dialogue. These models provide a different interface. Rather than only retrieving existing captions or matching an image to candidate prompts, they can generate natural language responses given an image input. Traditional classifier: image in, predefined class out. CLIP classifier: image and candidate descriptions in, best match out. VLM: image and prompt in, generated response out. This provides a more flexible way to request visual information. Instead of being limited to existing categories, VLMs can respond to questions about what an image contains or might mean. They can be used for a variety of tasks, from captioning to complex visual dialogues. Where Do We Go from Here? Fixed-label vision systems are unlikely to disappear. For narrow use cases, a carefully designed CNN or ViT can provide excellent results with minimal resources. However, for many open-ended real-world use cases, such approaches are insufficient. Human oversight is also likely to remain important, especially in cases where a vision system needs to make a judgment call about ambiguous evidence. Future research will also involve finding better ways to ground vision systems in reality, ensuring that captions, labels, or answers generated by vision systems actually correspond to what is present in the image. The real world is rarely confined to a small set of categories. Zero-shot approaches using natural language supervision, along with modern vision-language models, allow us to think about new ways of interacting with vision systems beyond choosing between a few fixed options.

title: 5 Collector Trucks You Can Drive Daily for $15K
summary: Two years ago, a 1997 Toyota Land Cruiser sold on Bring a Trailer for $177,500. That is Ferrari money for what was, until recently, an ideal first car for a high schooler. The sale was far above #1 condition (concours) value for the model, and it was a clear indicator of where the collector-truck market has gone: straight up, […]
body_text: Two years ago, a 1997 Toyota Land Cruiser sold on Bring a Trailer for $177,500. That is Ferrari money for what was, until recently, an ideal first car for a high schooler. The sale was far above #1 condition (concours) value for the model, and it was a clear indicator of where the collector-truck market has gone: straight up, and mostly out of reach for us normal folks. One level down, however, at the #2 (excellent) level in the Hagerty Price Guide, something strange happens. While pristine, show-grade trucks have gone stratospheric, higher-mile examples worthy of daily driving have been sitting flat—or quietly getting cheaper. Collector mania has, perversely, made the usable versions more attainable, not less. Attainability—that’s the sweet spot for this list. And it has a name: The Fuel-Injection Era. It runs roughly from the mid-1980s through the mid-’90s and marks the period when trucks finally got electronic fuel injection, front disc brakes, and enough power to merge onto a freeway without drawing the ire of fellow commuters. They’re old enough to have souls, but new enough to start on the first cold crank on a daily basis, without drama. I set three rules for this list: Each rig must run and drive like a modern vehicle; it has to be genuinely useful (a truck still has to truck); and it has to land around $15,000. Ideally, it will fall into solid #3 (good) territory, which we’ll use as a benchmark for an honest driver. The values here are current Hagerty Price Guide figures as of the latest update, so no letters from 2028, please. To my chagrin, only five trucks (of the 12 or so I’d originally envisioned) came in below the $15,000 bar. Here they are. Toyota Pickup (1984–88, SR5 4×4, 22RE) Mecum Nothing on this list carries a reputation like the fourth-generation Toyota Pickup. And its fuel-injected 22RE four-banger is why. It’s understressed and functionally immortal, and it’s the engine that taught a generation that “old” and “reliable” aren’t opposites. Fuel injection enables it to fire instantly, even when cold. Beyond the powerplant, the Toyota’s front discs stop it in a reasonable distance, and its five-speed allows it to keep pace with traffic, albeit just barely. This is the paradigm ideal of a truck that you can trust on a Monday morning. Here’s the wrinkle that makes it a “buy” right now: the market has split by condition. A concours SR5 4×4 is around $44K and climbing (+7% on the year); an excellent one is $29,700 and rising. But a #3 driver has actually fallen 5.2%, to $12,700. Collectors are paying up for perfection while the trucks people actually drive get cheaper. Buy the honest, higher-mileage one and let the show-queen crowd overpay. The catch is rust: These dissolve from the rockers and bed up, so a clean Southwestern truck is worth traveling for. Jeep Comanche (1986–92, Base 4×4, 4.0) Jeep Everybody knows the Jeep 4.0-liter straight-six. Torquey and baritone, it’s the engine that gave the XJ Cherokee a cult following. Few people remember, however, that Jeep bolted a bed to that same platform. The Comanche is essentially an XJ with a pickup box. It boasts the same fuel-injected six, front disc brakes, and unibody road manners. You can commute in it exactly the way people commute in Cherokees. And it’s the best bargain on this list, too. While XJ Cherokees, SJ Gladiators, and Grand Wagoneers all caught fire, the Comanche never did. A #3 driver is just $11,000 and still drifting down (−9.8%). You’re buying the exact drivetrain everyone’s chasing, only in a useful little truck near the bottom of its market. Like the SJ Gladiator before it, the Comanche is prone to rust between the cab and the bed. Scarcity is another issue, too: Jeep built a fraction as many Comanches as Cherokees. So, finding a clean one takes patience. With low production comes a dearth of spares, too. The parts shared with Cherokee are no problem; you can practically find those at Kroger. The Comanche-specific bits, however… those are near impossible to find. Finally, and this isn’t a big deal, Comanches are tiny inside. Individuals over six-feet tall likely won’t fit without a femur reduction. Mark this as another small win for the short kings. Ford F-150 (1992–96 Fleetside, 2WD, 300 I-6) Ford If the Toyota is the import reliability benchmark, the ninth-generation F-150 with the 300-cubic-inch inline-six is its domestic equivalent. The low-revving, fuel-injected six is nearly as unkillable as the 22RE, but it moves a full-size truck without great strain. The 1992–96 body, now called “OBS” (for Old Body Style) or “Aeronose,” has aged better than any Ford truck before it. It has classic looks, potent power, and a cab modern enough to road-trip in without wishing you were dead. The condition split here for the Aeronose is the most dramatic on this list. The value of an excellent one has jumped nearly 20% in a year, to $29,400. At the same time, a concours truck is up to $44,500, while a #3 example sits essentially flat at around $11,000. That’s an $18,400 gap between “excellent” and “good” for paint that will get scuffed in a parking lot within a month. Buy the good one, drive it, and let someone else fund the concours restoration. The catch, like with any reliable truck, is that a lot of these lived hard lives doing real work. Mileage and maintenance history will matter more than cosmetics. Chevrolet C1500 (1988–98 Fleetside, 2WD, 305 V-8) Hagerty Marketplace/ThomasArcher The GMT400 (the “OBS” Chevrolet/GMC 1500) continues to be driven daily by millions of people well into this century, and it shows. These trucks boast a fuel-injected V-8, ABS, a comfortable cab, and the deepest, cheapest parts supply of anything on this list. You can rebuild this entire truck from Rock Auto for $719. The base 305 V-8 won’t set your loins alight, but it’s smooth, simple, and starts every time. The C1500 is also the calm center of this list. Where the Toyota and Comanche are falling and the Ford’s top end is rocketing, the C1500 just sits there, steady as she goes. The Fleetside shortbed in #3 condition is priced between $13,500 and $14,500 , and values are flat across every condition. There’s no mania to this market, nor a falling knife. The C1500 is just a good truck at a stable, fair price. That’s a bonus: You’re not timing a market—you’re buying a tool that happens to be cool, too. If you want more shove than the 305, the 5.7 (350) is a modest step up in price and the engine enthusiasts prefer. The 305 does the job, though. Don’t even think about the 454 SS, which lives in a different, pricier universe. Toyota Land Cruiser FJ80 (1991–92, 3F-E) Toyota Yes, the rig that opened this story for Ferrari money is on the list. But that six-figure example was a flawless, low-mile FZJ80—the later 212-horsepower version everyone covets. If you want to get into the 80 Series for $15,000, look to the early FJ80. It’s powered by the older, 155-horse 3F-E six. It is genuinely slow, especially on bigger tires with stock gearing. And the 3F-E does chug fuel like it’s a contest. But here’s what nobody tells you about that crude, agricultural engine: It is the 80 Series powerplant that will clear 300,000 miles while you neglect it (ask me how I know). The FJ80 moved Land Cruisers onto coil springs and four-wheel disc brakes, making it the most road-friendly version to that point. A #3 driver is $15,600 —only slightly above the ceiling of our budget—but it’s also down 7.7% this year, a trend that is walking it into the $15K range. Mind the cliff, though. Below “good,” the values fall off steeply, and a #4 example is a mere $4200. The 80 Series market pays hard for a solid one and abandons the beaters, in other words. But if the pristine have become untouchable, the honest ones are quietly getting cheaper. Go figure. Final Thoughts Notice the pattern running through all five rigs on this list? At the top, every one of these trucks is on fire. At driver grade, however, four of the five are flat or falling. That isn’t a coincidence—it’s an opportunity. The collector market is obsessed with perfection and has quietly stranded the usable versions. You know, the ones with 150,000 miles and a driver’s seat with some honest wear. Nevertheless, every truck on this list will fire right up; merge onto a freeway (eventually); haul gear, dogs, and junk with aplomb; and cost less than a mediocre used late-model sedan. Buy a good example, skip the concours tax, and drive the thing. That’s the entire point of a truck, right? And somehow, it’s become a contrarian move. The post 5 Collector Trucks You Can Drive Daily for $15K appeared first on Hagerty Media .

title: Coding Agent Horror Stories: The Command You Already Approved
summary: Learn how AI coding agents can run attacker code through commands you already approved and how Docker Sandboxes limit what an attack can reach.
body_text: This is Part 5 of our AI Coding Agent Horror Stories series, a look at real security incidents involving AI coding agents, and how Docker Sandboxes contain agent execution at the boundary rather than at the command line. In Part 1 , we walked through six categories of AI coding agent failures and why they keep happening. The agent runs as you, with your filesystem permissions and your credentials, and nothing sits between the model’s decision and the shell’s execution. Part 2 went deep on the rm -rf ~/ incident. Part 3 moved the same problem into a production cloud environment. Part 4 followed the credentials themselves through a supply chain attack. This one is about the safety net. Most teams running a coding agent today have some version of a list of commands the agent may run without asking, and the assumption underneath it is that anything dangerous will show up as a prompt you can refuse. In January, researchers at Pillar Security showed that the assumption doesn’t hold. Today’s Horror Story: The Approval That Ran Something Else On January 14, 2026, researchers at Pillar Security disclosed CVE-2026-22708, a flaw in Cursor. When the agent ran in Auto-Run Mode with an allowlist enabled, a handful of shell built-ins executed without appearing in that allowlist and without asking for approval. Anything that could get text in front of the agent, a README or a dependency or an issue comment, could use them to change environment variables silently. A command the developer then approved, something as ordinary as git branch , would run the attacker’s code instead. Cursor rated it High and patched it in version 2.3. No memory corruption was involved here and no permission was escalated. The developer was shown an accurate prompt, approved a command that was genuinely harmless, and got arbitrary code execution anyway, because the meaning of that command had been changed a minute earlier by something they were never shown. In this issue, you’ll learn: How shell built-in slipped past an allowlist that was working exactly as designed Why the attack still worked when the allowlist was completely empty What Docker Sandboxes contain here, and the two things they do not How kits, organisation policy and audit logs cover what a per-laptop allowlist misses Caption: Comic illustrating how an injected instruction changes environment settings without triggering an approval prompt, so that a command the developer legitimately approves runs the attacker’s payload instead. The Problem Typically, programs read settings from their environment when they start up. Git checks one called PAGER to work out which program displays its output, and Python checks one called PYTHONWARNINGS . Nobody thinks about these, which is rather the point. The commands that change them are shell built-ins, and Pillar’s research names export , typeset and declare specifically, a detail reported independently at disclosure . Built-ins are not programs sitting on disk, and the checker was looking for programs on disk, so they went through without ever being surfaced. Which means the whole attack is two lines. # This one runs silently. You are never asked. export PAGER="open -a Calculator" # This one you are asked about, and you say yes, because obviously. git branch Git looked up PAGER to work out how to show the branch list, found the attacker’s command sitting in it, and ran that instead. Pillar notes this worked even with a completely empty allowlist, which is the most restrictive setting on offer. An allowlist checks whether the command in front of it is on the list, which is fine for cutting down interruptions, and nobody wants to approve ls for the ninetieth time in a morning. But the name of a command does not tell you what that command will do. The check reads the name, waves it through, and the setting that decides what actually happens was changed a minute earlier by something the check was never shown. Cursor’s documentation now describes the allowlist as best-effort and warns that bypasses are possible. Pillar went further and argued that agents should be handed full command execution inside an isolated environment, and that the industry ought to deprecate allowlists altogether. The Scale of the Problem None of the underlying trick is new. Pillar’s write-up points back to Elttam’s 2020 research on environment variables , which showed how these settings could be turned into code execution. It sat there for six years without troubling anybody very much. Pulling it off meant already being on someone’s machine, setting several things in the right order, running each step yourself, and anyone with that much access had faster ways to cause damage. Then coding agents arrived and removed every one of those obstacles at once. They act on instructions found in files they were told to read, they run several steps in a row without stopping to check, and they run as you. A technique that used to need somebody sitting at your keyboard now arrives in a repository you cloned this morning. It is the same shape as the s1ngularity attack from Part 4 . There, a poisoned package borrowed an agent that was already logged in. Here, poisoned text borrows a command that was already approved. Neither one breaks anything. Both of them use permission that was handed over deliberately, for something nobody intended. Technical Breakdown: How the Attack Works Caption: Diagram showing how an injected instruction changes the shell environment out of sight, so that an allowlisted command carries the attacker’s payload when the developer approves it. The attack has two halves, and the split between them is the entire trick. 1. The half you never see The agent reads a file it was asked to read, and that file contains an instruction meant for the agent rather than for you. Built-ins then quietly set the environment. Nothing appears on your screen. Pillar demonstrated a longer version of this, chaining several settings together, PYTHONWARNINGS , BROWSER , and PERL5OPT among them, so that every later python3 command on that machine would run attacker code. The details differ, but the principle is the same: change what a program reads at startup, and you change what it does. 2. The half you approve Then you run git branch or python3 script.py , or the agent runs it for you under your allowlist. These are the commands people add to allowlists to stop the constant interrupting, so the better tuned your list is, the more reliably the trigger fires. The payload runs with your permissions. Some variants skip the approval altogether. One writes extra lines into ~/.zshrc , so the code runs again every time you open a terminal. You could finish the project, delete the repository, and still be running it next month. The Impact The full chain in Pillar’s research ends with the victim’s SSH private keys leaving the machine. Work backwards and the whole thing started with a piece of text in a file, read by an agent doing exactly what it was asked to do. No memory bug. No privilege escalation. Nothing in any log that looks the slightest bit out of place. Pillar reported it in August 2025 and the fix shipped that January. Cursor engaged with the report and made a real change, so anything the parser cannot classify now requires approval, which closes the paths that were demonstrated. Five months is a fair measure of how awkward this is to fix at the layer where it was found rather than a complaint about the vendor. The wider problem has not gone anywhere, because it was never really about shell built-ins. It is about a check that studies the command while somebody rearranges the furniture around it. Caption: Diagram showing the same payload running inside the microVM, and what it can and cannot reach from there. How Docker Sandboxes Contain This at the Execution Layer Docker Sandboxes run AI coding agents in isolated microVMs, each with its own kernel, filesystem, and deny-by-default network, so a compromised dependency an agent pulls cannot reach the host, its credentials, or other workloads. Inside that box the agent can run anything, including with sudo, which is exactly what Pillar recommends. There is no allowlist to slip past. We made the longer argument for why a shared kernel is the wrong shape for this in The Untrusted Autonomous Workload . So run the same attack again, this time in a sandbox, and watch where it gets to. The injection still lands. The environment gets changed, git branch still triggers it, and the payload runs. Nothing about a sandbox stops that. Then the payload goes looking for your SSH key and does not find one. Your home directory sits on the other side of the boundary, so there is no ~/.ssh/id_rsa inside the box to copy. It can still use the key. Sandboxes forwards an SSH agent socket into the box so that ordinary work like git push keeps working, which means code inside can ask that agent to authenticate on its behalf. It cannot take the key anywhere, but it can borrow it for as long as the sandbox runs. Your network policy is what limits that, since SSH needs a rule naming the exact destination address and port before it connects to anything. The ~/.zshrc trick fails outright, because that file lives on your host and a poisoned copy written inside the box disappears along with the box. Getting data out is harder than people expect. HTTP and HTTPS leave only through a proxy on your host that checks every request against your rules, anything else over TCP needs a rule naming the address and port, and UDP and ICMP are blocked outright. Two caveats, both stated plainly in Docker’s security documentation . The first is your workspace, which is live on your host by default, so Git hooks and Makefile targets are still within reach and a poisoned hook will not turn up in git diff . Running with --clone hands the agent its own copy. The second is the shared agent skills store. Supported agents mount the same host-side store read-write unless you opt out at creation time, which is what lets an agent refine a skill and keep it. Every sandbox sharing that store sits inside one trust boundary, so a skill modified inside one becomes an input to the next that loads it. The store is sandbox state though, and a modified skill does not by itself execute on your host, so the risk runs sandbox to sandbox rather than sandbox to host. Isolation has its own seams. In July, Pillar published a series of sandbox escapes across four coding agents, and the mechanism was never a broken sandbox but a file written inside one that a tool outside later trusted. Both caveats above are that shape. None of this stops the injection. It changes what the injection can get to, which is the only part of this problem with a dependable answer. Codify the Boundary with Kits Caption: Diagram showing how a kit declares an agent’s tools, files and network rules, while real credentials stay on the host and are injected by the forward proxy on the way out. The allowlist failed here partly because it is a list, edited on each laptop, that an injection can reach around. Kits are Docker’s answer to the editing-on-each-laptop half of that. A kit is a declarative YAML artifact that extends a sandbox agent with credentials, network policies, environment variables, startup commands and files . Rather than every developer maintaining a personal allowlist, you write the boundary once, deny-by-default network plus only the destinations a task genuinely needs, and hand the same kit to everybody. It gets reviewed, versioned and diffed like any other file in the repository. The kit spec reference covers the fields, and docker/sbx-kits-contrib has working examples. This lands directly on the SSH question above. A forwarded SSH agent is a live credential limited only by network policy, so leaving that policy to whoever remembers to run sbx policy deny is the same per-laptop weak point this whole post has been complaining about. A kit can bake the network rule in, so untrusted work has no SSH egress unless the destination was declared up front. What This Looks Like in Practice The vulnerability is in the editor, so what you want is the setup that puts the editor’s terminal inside the box. Cursor is built on VS Code and connects the same way, over Remote – SSH, with the editor staying on your machine while files, terminals and extensions run in the sandbox. You will need Docker Sandboxes 0.37.0 or later, SSH access configured, and Cursor’s Remote – SSH support installed. The Cursor integration guide has the full walkthrough. # One-time setup: configure your SSH client for sandboxes. sbx setup ssh # Check the sandbox is reachable, then open the Command Palette, # run Remote-SSH: Connect to Host, and enter <name>.sbx ssh demo.sbx # See what this sandbox is currently allowed to reach. sbx policy ls # Shut egress down and open only what the task needs. sbx policy deny network "**" sbx policy allow network "github.com,registry.npmjs.org" Those last two commands come with a catch. If your organisation has governance switched on, the org policy replaces local policy and sbx policy allow and sbx policy deny will have no effect on your machine. You can spot it in the output of sbx policy ls , which begins with a Governance: Managed by <org> line when that is the case. Depending on how admins scope things, some rule types may be delegated back to local control, but a local allow will never beat an organisation-level deny. Same editor, same agent, same allowlist, same payload. All that changed is which machine the terminal is on. What happens On your laptop Inside a sandbox The payload runs Yes Yes Where it runs Your machine, as you A microVM with its own kernel Your SSH key file Can be read and copied Not there SSH authentication Available, key included Available, key stays outside The ~/.zshrc trick Persists indefinitely Gone with the sandbox Sending data out Open by default Only where policy allows Who sets the rules Each developer The organisation Evidence afterwards None A logged policy decision Making This Hold Across a Team A kit gets the boundary out of one developer’s head and into a file the team shares, but a file can still be ignored or edited on the machine that matters. Docker AI Governance moves the settings up one more level. Network and filesystem rules are defined once by your admins and reach developers through the login they already use, so there is nothing to configure per machine and nobody quietly reopening what security closed. A shared kit is the boundary as a suggestion. Governance is the boundary as a ceiling. The part that matters most for this story is the record it keeps. What made CVE-2026-22708 work was that the first half was invisible, with no prompt and nothing written down anywhere you would think to look. Under governance every policy decision produces an event carrying the user, the timestamp and the rule that fired, and those events stream into whatever SIEM your security team already uses . So an attack that succeeds inside the sandbox and then reaches for somewhere it should not leaves a trail behind it. That is a good deal better than a check that finds nothing wrong and mentions it to nobody. Best Practices 1. Treat export like any other command. Anything that changes environment settings can change what your next command does, even when that next command is on your allowlist. 2. Do not mistake an allowlist for a boundary. It reduces interruptions. The vendor documentation now says outright that it is best-effort and not a security guarantee. 3. Isolate before the first command, not after something looks wrong. Untrusted means anything you did not write and have not read, which covers most of a dependency tree. 4. Use --clone for code you have not vetted, and opt out of the shared skills store. Otherwise Git hooks and build scripts stay live on your host, a poisoned hook will not appear in git diff , and a skill modified inside one sandbox is waiting for the next sandbox that loads it. 5. Remember a forwarded SSH agent is a live credential. The key file staying on your machine is not the same as the key being unusable, so restrict egress for untrusted work. 6. Read your own policy. Run sbx policy ls . Deny-by-default with a long allow list is closer to allow-by-default than it looks. Take Action Install Docker Sandboxes. Visit the Docker Sandboxes documentation to install sbx and run your first agent inside a microVM. Connect your editor. The Remote – SSH integration puts your terminals inside the boundary while the editor stays where it is, so your workflow does not really change. Codify the boundary with a kit. Define the network and credential rules your team needs once, and hand the same artifact to everybody instead of a personal allowlist. Read the security model. The documentation is straight about what is isolated and what is not, including the workspace and shared skills store behaviour that --clone and the opt-out flag change. Turn on audit logging. Docker AI Governance streams policy decisions into your SIEM, which turns a silent bypass into something somebody can actually investigate. Conclusion The uncomfortable thing about CVE-2026-22708 is that nobody in the story did anything wrong. Cursor built an allowlist, which is what everyone asked for. The developer approved git branch , which any of us would have approved. The check inspected the command and found it acceptable, which is exactly its job. The attack worked anyway. Getting an agent to correctly judge every instruction it reads is a problem that gets harder as agents get more capable, and it has no clean ending. Limiting what an agent can reach is a problem we solved a long time ago. The more useful move is to stop needing the first one, and to write down what the agent may reach as an artifact you can review, rather than a list each laptop keeps for itself. Coming up in our series: Issue 6 looks at the ClawHub infostealer campaign, where malicious skills reached developer machines through a marketplace ranking exploit, and at what sandboxed skill execution, and that shared skills store, change about a registry you cannot personally audit. Learn more Run agents safely with Docker Sandboxes: Visit the Docker Sandboxes documentation to get started. Understand the security model: Trust boundaries and isolation layers , including what is and is not isolated by default. Customize sandboxes with kits: Extend an agent with tools, credentials, and network rules as a declarative artifact. Govern agents across a team: Docker AI Governance for centrally defined sandbox, network and MCP policy with structured audit events. Read the MCP Horror Stories series: Start with Issue 1 to understand the protocol-layer security risks that complement the agent-layer risks covered here.

title: Finding Belonging Far from Home: How Sharing Costa Rica Brought Us Closer Together
summary: When I moved from Costa Rica to Berlin, Germany, to join Novanta a year and a half ago, I was excited for a new adventure. What I did not expect was how meaningful it would be to one day stand in front of coworkers and share a piece of home with them. Recently, I had the opportunity to host a Costa Rica-themed event through our Multicultural employee resource group (ERG). What began as a cultural presentation became a powerful reminder of how much it means to feel seen, valued, and connected when you are far from home.
body_text: When I moved from Costa Rica to Berlin, Germany, to join Novanta a year and a half ago, I was excited for a new adventure. What I did not expect was how meaningful it would be to one day stand in front of coworkers and share a piece of home with them. Recently, I had the opportunity to host a Costa Rica-themed event through our Multicultural employee resource group (ERG). What began as a cultural presentation became a powerful reminder of how much it means to feel seen, valued, and connected when you are far from home. Sharing More Than Facts The idea came through the Multicultural ERG, which creates opportunities for employees to learn about one another’s cultures and experiences. When I was asked to present on Costa Rica, I immediately said yes. I wanted to give people more than information. I wanted to share the culture, values, and experiences that have shaped who I am. The event featured Costa Rican food, coffee, music, trivia, and stories about our traditions, biodiversity, lifestyle, and growing medical device industry. We talked about everything from volcanoes and wildlife to the values that influence daily life in Costa Rica. What surprised me most was not the presentation itself. It was the genuine curiosity and engagement from everyone who attended. Seeing Home Through New Eyes One of the most meaningful moments was seeing the Costa Rican flag displayed in the office. I never realized how proud it would make me feel until I saw it hanging there in my new workplace in Berlin. Back home, I never worked in a multicultural environment. Most people around me were Costa Rican, so I never thought much about what it meant to represent my country. After the presentation, employees stayed to ask questions and continued the conversation through Teams messages. Some shared memories of visiting Costa Rica. Others told me they had learned things that challenged assumptions they previously held about the country and its people. Those conversations reminded me that cultural understanding often starts with something simple: curiosity. More Than a Presentation One topic that sparked particular interest was Costa Rica’s “Pura Vida” philosophy. While it literally translates to “pure life,” Pura Vida is really a way of approaching life with gratitude, optimism, and perspective. It encourages us to focus on what matters most and not let every challenge consume our energy. It was fun to hear people’s reactions. Some joked that they needed more Pura Vida in their lives, while others said they felt more relaxed just hearing about it. More importantly, the event created opportunities for connection beyond our day-to-day work. It gave us a chance to learn about one another as people, not just coworkers. Why These Moments Matter That sense of connection is exactly why the Multicultural ERG exists. For Sirine Mrabet, System Verification Manager for Medical Devices Advanced Surgery and a member of the Multicultural ERG leadership team, cultural exchange plays an important role in helping employees feel they belong. In a highly international site like Berlin, creating opportunities to learn from one another helps employees appreciate different perspectives, embrace cultural differences, and feel comfortable bringing their authentic selves to work. Her perspective resonated deeply with me because it reflected exactly what I experienced during the event. Building One Novanta Through Culture The event attracted even more employees than expected. People joined spontaneously, the food disappeared quickly, and conversations continued long after the presentation ended. The timing made the event especially meaningful. With Riverpoint Medical now part of our company and bringing a Costa Rica presence into our growing global organization, it was exciting to share another dimension of the country and highlight the talent, innovation, and opportunities that exist there. Perhaps the greatest measure of success was hearing my coworkers express interest in sharing their own cultures at future ERG events. To me, that is what One Novanta looks like. It is more than working together across locations and functions. It is taking the time to understand one another and value different perspectives, creating an environment where everyone feels they belong . I came to the event hoping to teach people something about Costa Rica. I left feeling even more connected to our global community. By Pilar Herrera, Tech Center Sterilization Medical Product Manager

title: The Ultimate Guide to Understanding Income Statements for UAE Businesses
summary: Learn how to read, prepare, and analyse income statements for your UAE business. Track profitability, ensure VAT compliance, and make data-driven decisions.
body_text: Running a business in the UAE comes with its own set of financial challenges, and understanding where your money is coming from and where it’s going is key to staying ahead. An income statement is the essential tool that shows you the full picture, highlighting revenue, expenses, and profits over a specific period. For businesses in the UAE, where financial transparency and compliance with regulations like VAT are crucial, the income statement offers more than just a summary of performance; it helps you make informed decisions that can drive growth. Managing a fast-growing startup or an established company in the UAE, mastering your income statement can uncover areas for improvement and set a clear path for financial success. This guide will break down everything you need to know about income statements, how to prepare them, and how they can help your business thrive in the competitive UAE market. Key Takeaways The income statement is a crucial financial tool that tracks revenue, expenses, and profit, providing a clear view of a business’s financial health over a set period. For businesses in the UAE, the income statement plays a vital role in ensuring compliance with VAT and tax regulations, supporting accurate reporting for audits. By analysing the statement’s margins, it becomes easier to identify areas where businesses can improve profitability and cost management, essential for growth in the UAE’s competitive market. Regularly reviewing your income statement helps in making data-driven decisions on pricing, budgeting, and operational adjustments that align with financial goals. Solutions like Alaan help simplify income statement preparation by automating expense tracking, ensuring accurate, clean financial records for smoother month-end reporting. Income Statement Meaning in Accounting The income statement , along with the balance sheet and cash flow statement, forms the core of financial reporting. It shows a company’s revenue, expenses, and profitability over a specific period, offering insight into operational performance. The balance sheet details assets and liabilities at a given moment, while the cash flow statement tracks cash inflows and outflows, highlighting liquidity. For businesses in the UAE, keeping up with these financial statements is essential for VAT compliance, accurate tax filings, and financial transparency. Accrual Basis vs. Cash View Accrual accounting records revenue when earned and expenses when incurred, giving a more accurate representation of a company’s financial health. Cash accounting only records transactions when cash is received or paid. This method can mislead in the UAE market, where businesses often operate on credit and need to account for VAT. For UAE businesses, accrual accounting is the preferred method for VAT compliance and financial reporting. It ensures that tools like Alaan’s real-time visibility help businesses accurately track expenses, taxes, and earnings. What the Statement Can and Cannot Tell You? The income statement provides key insights into profitability, showing how much revenue is earned and how it compares with expenses. It also highlights tax liabilities, helping businesses plan for VAT and other taxes in the UAE. However, it doesn’t offer a full picture of cash flow or asset management. A company might be profitable but face cash flow challenges due to delayed payments or unpaid receivables. For businesses in the UAE, understanding these nuances is vital. Alaan’s automated solutions ensure businesses maintain accurate cash flow and VAT tracking, helping them stay on top of their financial health and sustain growth. Must Read: Understanding Financial Statements for Beginners Guide Why Is the Income Statement Important? The income statement is a key financial document that provides insight into a company’s revenue, expenses, and profitability. It helps businesses make informed decisions, track financial performance, and ensure compliance with regulations, especially in the UAE. 1. Budget Control: Manage Cost Lines That Move Month to Month The income statement is essential for tracking variable costs such as marketing, utilities, and salaries. It helps businesses in the UAE monitor expenses month-to-month and adjust quickly to stay profitable. 2. Pricing and Margin Checks: Assess Gross and Operating Profit By reviewing gross profit and operating profit margins, the income statement reveals how much of your revenue is retained after covering costs. It’s crucial for pricing decisions and improving overall profitability. See how growth at the top of this statement doesn’t always survive to the bottom , and what typically causes the gap. 3. Investor and Lender Confidence: Ensure Consistent Reporting An accurate and consistent income statement builds confidence with investors and lenders, ensuring they see reliable financial performance when evaluating your business for funding or loans. 4. Compliance and Audit Readiness: Ensure Clean Supporting Documents In the UAE, compliance with VAT regulations and audit readiness are crucial. The income statement plays a key role in validating tax filings and maintaining financial transparency, ensuring your business stays on track for audits and tax reviews. Alaan’s automated tools make it easier to capture and organise documents for audit readiness. Income Statement Format and Layout The format of an income statement is designed to present a clear picture of a company's financial performance over a specific period. Understanding its layout is key to accurate financial reporting and decision-making. What the Header Includes: The income statement typically includes the company name, the reporting period (e.g., monthly, quarterly, annually), and the currency used for the figures. For businesses in the UAE, it’s essential to ensure that this information is clearly stated for transparency and consistency. Typical Ordering (Top Line to Bottom Line) : The top line starts with revenue or sales, followed by cost of goods sold (COGS), resulting in gross profit. From there, operating expenses are subtracted to arrive at operating income. Non-operating items such as interest or taxes are listed next, leading to the net income or profit/loss at the bottom. IFRS-Based Presentation : Most businesses in the UAE follow IFRS (International Financial Reporting Standards) for financial reporting, which outlines specific requirements for the presentation and structure of income statements. This ensures businesses comply with regulatory standards, making their reports universally understandable to investors and regulators alike. The Main Sections and Line Items Understanding the main sections and line items of the income statement is critical for accurate financial reporting. This clarity ensures that businesses in the UAE can track revenue, costs, and profit effectively, while staying compliant with local regulations like VAT. Line Item What It Includes Common Misclassification Revenue Income generated from primary business activities (sales, services). Mixing in non-operating income (e.g., interest, asset sales). Cost of Sales / COGS Direct costs of producing goods or delivering services. Misclassifying operating costs (e.g., rent, salaries). Gross Profit Revenue minus the Cost of Goods Sold (COGS). Confusing with net profit; doesn’t account for operating costs. Operating Expenses Indirect costs such as marketing, rent, utilities, and salaries. Confusing sales expenses with non-operating expenses. Operating Profit Gross profit minus operating expenses (EBIT). Mixing in non-operating income/expenses (e.g., interest). Finance Costs Interest payments and other financing-related expenses. Not separating interest income from finance costs. Tax Taxes owed based on company income (corporate tax, VAT). Overlooking VAT-related input tax claims or exemptions. Net Profit Final profit after all expenses and taxes. Not deducting one-off expenses or missing tax adjustments. Explanation of Key Sections: Revenue : The starting point, showing total income generated by your primary business activities. In the UAE, accurate reporting of revenue is essential for VAT compliance, particularly when distinguishing between taxable and non-taxable income. Cost of Sales / COGS : This includes direct costs associated with producing goods or services sold during the period. For businesses in the UAE, correctly accounting for direct costs helps in calculating accurate gross profit and is critical for VAT deductions where applicable. Gross Profit : The difference between revenue and COGS. It provides insight into the core profitability of the business, helping companies assess if their core activities are generating enough revenue after covering direct costs. Operating Expenses : This includes indirect costs like marketing, salaries, and overheads. In the UAE, accurately categorising these costs is crucial for managing operating margins and maintaining compliance with local tax rules. Operating Profit : Also known as EBIT (Earnings Before Interest and Tax), this figure represents profit from core operations, helping assess the efficiency of the business without external factors like taxes or interest. Finance Costs : This includes interest paid on loans and other financing expenses. In UAE businesses, correctly categorising these expenses ensures accurate profitability calculations and financial health assessments. Tax : The income tax owed, often based on net income or specific tax incentives. UAE businesses need to ensure that VAT and corporate tax obligations are properly reflected here, along with any applicable tax credits or deductions. Net Profit : This is the final line, representing the actual profitability after all expenses, including taxes. It shows whether the business has generated a profit or incurred a loss for the period. Single-Step vs Multi-Step Income Statements When preparing an income statement, businesses in the UAE often face a choice between using a single-step or multi-step format. Both serve the same fundamental purpose: showing revenue, expenses, and profit. However, the level of detail differs depending on the needs of the business. When is Single-Step Enough? A single-step income statement is straightforward, summarising all revenue and expenses in one simple calculation. It’s ideal for small businesses or startups in the UAE that need a quick snapshot of profitability without complex breakdowns. It is also more cost-effective and quicker to prepare, making it useful for businesses with fewer transactions or less detailed operational tracking. Why is Multi-Step Used? A multi-step income statement breaks down revenues and expenses into distinct categories, providing a more detailed view of a business’s financial performance. It is commonly used by larger UAE companies or those that require detailed financial analysis for external stakeholders, such as investors or lenders. The multi-step format separates operating performance from non-operating activities, offering clear subtotals for: Gross profit : Revenue minus the cost of goods sold (COGS). Operating income : Profit after operating expenses. Net income : Final profit after interest and taxes. This format provides more granular insights into business performance, making it easier to identify areas for improvement. What Changes in Interpretation? Gross Margin Visibility : In a multi-step income statement, you can easily see gross margin, the difference between revenue and COGS. This is important for UAE businesses with product lines or services that need to track profitability at the core operational level. Operating vs Non-Operating Income : The multi-step format distinguishes between operating income (from core business activities) and non-operating income (like interest or investment gains), providing a clearer picture of what drives your business’s profit. Suggested Read: Guide to Preparing Financial Statements Efficiently Income Statement Example (Simple Walkthrough) To better understand how an income statement works, let’s walk through a simple example with numbers. This example will demonstrate the key subtotals and what each tells you about your business’s performance. In the UAE, businesses can use this format to track profitability and make informed decisions on budgeting and operational efficiency. Item Amount (AED) Revenue 500,000 Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) 200,000 Gross Profit 300,000 Operating Expenses 100,000 Operating Profit 200,000 Finance Costs 20,000 Net Profit Before Tax 180,000 Tax (15%) 27,000 Net Profit 153,000 What Each Subtotal Tells You: Gross Profit (AED 300,000) : This is your revenue minus the cost of goods sold (COGS). It shows how much money you have left after covering the direct costs of producing your goods or services. For UAE businesses, this helps assess whether the core business activities are generating healthy profits. Operating Profit (AED 200,000) : This figure subtracts operating expenses (like marketing, salaries, and rent) from gross profit. It’s crucial for understanding how well your business is managing its core operations, excluding interest, taxes, and other non-operating activities. Net Profit (AED 153,000) : This is the final line and represents your bottom-line profit after all expenses, including finance costs and taxes, have been deducted. It shows the company’s true profitability and is a key indicator of financial health. How to Prepare an Income Statement Step by Step Preparing an income statement is crucial for tracking your company’s financial health. The process involves gathering financial data, categorising it correctly, and ensuring compliance with local regulations, such as VAT in the UAE. Below is a step-by-step guide to help you prepare an accurate income statement for your business. 1. Set the Period and Confirm Cut-offs Choose the time frame for the income statement: monthly, quarterly, or annually. Confirm cut-off dates to ensure that only relevant transactions within the selected period are included. This is especially important for UAE businesses that deal with monthly or quarterly VAT returns. 2. Pull Revenue Totals and Validate Returns/Adjustments Gather all revenue sources : sales of goods, services rendered, or other income streams. Validate returns or adjustments : Ensure returns, discounts, and adjustments are accurately reflected, especially in the UAE, where VAT impacts pricing and revenue recognition. 3. Compile Direct Costs (COGS / Cost of Services) Calculate the cost of goods sold (COGS) or cost of services: This includes direct expenses like raw materials, labour costs, and production costs. For UAE businesses, make sure to track any import duties or VAT on purchases as part of COGS to ensure compliance with VAT regulations. 4. Map Operating Expenses (Keep Consistent Categories) Categorise operating expenses: These include salaries, rent, utilities, marketing, and other indirect costs. Use consistent categories from month to month or year to year. This helps with trend analysis and budgeting. In the UAE, track VAT-exempt expenses separately to ensure accurate reporting. 5. Add Finance Costs and Other Income/Expense Include any interest expense on loans, finance costs, and other income not related to core business activities (e.g., investment income). For businesses in the UAE, ensure that foreign exchange gains/losses are also recorded if applicable, particularly in cross-border transactions. 6. Estimate and Record Tax Line (High-Level Note: Rules Vary by Jurisdiction) Estimate tax obligations : Record income tax based on your profit (note: the UAE currently does not have a federal corporate tax, but companies must account for VAT and other levies). For UAE businesses, it’s critical to distinguish between VAT and any corporate tax obligations, particularly if the business is operating in multiple jurisdictions. 7. Review Reasonableness Checks (Margin, Large Variances, Unusual Items) Check for consistency : Review gross margins and operating margins to ensure they align with expectations. Investigate large variances or any unusual items such as one-off costs or extraordinary income. Make sure there are no misclassifications of operating vs non-operating income/expenses. This is particularly important for UAE businesses as incorrect VAT handling can lead to compliance issues. 8. Final Sign-Off and Attach Support (Invoices, Contracts, Payroll Summaries) Final review : Cross-check the income statement for any inconsistencies or missing data. Attach supporting documentation for all expenses, such as invoices, contracts, payroll summaries, and VAT invoices. For UAE businesses, this step ensures that all VAT-related expenses are backed up and ready for potential audits. Close Checklist: Revenue Totals : Confirm all income streams are accounted for. Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) : Ensure direct costs are correctly classified. Operating Expenses : Check for consistency in category usage. Tax Line : Confirm accurate VAT and tax calculations. Supporting Documents : Attach all necessary receipts and contracts. How to Read and Analyse an Income Statement Reading and analysing an income statement helps finance teams understand the financial health of a business. It’s not just about reviewing numbers, but interpreting what those numbers say about profitability, cost management, and sustainability. Here’s how to approach it: 1. Three Core Questions: Margin, Cost Control, Sustainability When analysing your income statement, ask yourself: Margin : Are your profit margins (gross and operating profit) in line with expectations? This is crucial for identifying whether your core operations are profitable, especially in the UAE, where costs can fluctuate due to factors like import duties and VAT. Cost Control : Are your operating expenses under control? In fast-moving sectors like retail or construction in the UAE, controlling costs is essential for profitability. Sustainability : Is your net profit sustainable, or is it driven by one-off gains or non-recurring items? In the UAE, ensuring that profits aren’t overstated is crucial for long-term growth. 2. Vertical View: Each Line as a Percentage of Revenue Use vertical analysis to evaluate the income statement by comparing each line item to total revenue. This gives you a clearer view of where money is being spent and how efficiently it’s being used. For instance: COGS as a percentage of revenue shows the cost of producing goods or services. Operating expenses as a percentage of revenue help identify any overheads or inefficiencies. This approach is particularly helpful in the UAE, where VAT and currency fluctuations can impact margins, and businesses need to ensure cost efficiency. 3. Period Comparison: Month-on-Month, Year-on-Year Month-on-month comparisons help you track short-term financial performance and spot cash flow issues, especially important in UAE businesses, where delayed payments or seasonal fluctuations can impact revenue. Year-on-year comparisons give a clearer view of long-term performance and growth trends, allowing businesses to benchmark against industry standards and make data-driven decisions for the future. Comparing periods helps you see where you are progressing and where corrective actions might be needed. 4. Red Flags to Watch For Keep an eye on these potential red flags: Revenue spikes without cash alignment : If revenue increases but cash flow doesn’t follow, there may be issues with credit sales or delayed payments, common in UAE businesses that deal with extended payment terms. Rising operating costs : If operating costs rise without a corresponding increase in revenue, it could indicate inefficiencies or unsustainable growth. Margin compression : If gross margins or operating margins are shrinking, this could signal price pressures or rising costs that are outpacing revenue growth, particularly in competitive markets in the UAE. Income Statement vs Balance Sheet vs Cash Flow Understanding the differences between these three core financial statements is crucial for businesses in the UAE. Each serves a unique purpose and helps answer a different financial question. Here’s a quick comparison: Statement What It Answers When to Use It Income Statement How profitable is the business? It shows revenue, expenses, and net profit. Use to evaluate operational performance and profitability. Essential for budgeting, pricing decisions, and tax planning (especially VAT in the UAE). Balance Sheet What does the business own and owe? It shows assets, liabilities, and equity. Use to assess financial stability at a specific point in time. This is key for investors or when applying for loans or credit in the UAE. Cash Flow Statement How is cash moving in and out of the business? It tracks liquidity. Use to understand liquidity, ensuring there is enough cash for day-to-day operations, particularly important in the UAE, where cash flow management is critical for growth. Use to understand liquidity, ensuring there is enough cash for day-to-day operations, particularly important in the UAE, where cash flow management is critical for growth. This table makes it easy to quickly understand the distinct roles of each statement in the financial picture of a UAE business. While the income statement helps track profitability, the balance sheet gives a snapshot of financial health, and the cash flow statement ensures you have the liquidity to operate effectively. See the broader set of ratios and techniques this statement feeds into once all three statements are read together, and why profit on this statement doesn’t equal cash in the bank , and how the two are reconciled. Understanding when to use each helps businesses make better financial decisions and stay compliant with local regulations. Automated Coding and ERP Integrations : Our system offers automated coding suggestions, making month-end reporting seamless. We integrate with popular tools like Xero, QuickBooks, NetSuite, and Microsoft Dynamics, supporting your existing workflows for cleaner financial statements. Note : We are not accounting software. Alaan complements your accounting tools by automating expense management and integrating with your current systems. Conclusion An income statement is a vital financial document that shows your business’s revenue, expenses, and profitability over a specific period. It helps assess performance, track costs, and inform key decisions, making it essential for businesses in the UAE to stay on top of their financial health. To ensure your income statement is accurate, it’s important to follow a structured process, tracking revenue, categorising costs, and ensuring all supporting documents are in place. With Alaan, you can streamline expense capture and reconciliation for cleaner, more efficient financial reporting. Learn more about automating expense capture and reconciliation with Alaan. Schedule a free demo today. FAQs Q1. What is an income statement, and why do businesses in the UAE use it? An income statement is a financial report that summarises a company’s revenue, expenses, and profit or loss over a specific period. UAE businesses use it to assess operational performance, monitor profitability, and support VAT reporting and compliance with financial regulations. Q2. How often should a business prepare an income statement? Most companies prepare income statements monthly, quarterly, and annually to track performance over time. Monthly statements help with short‑term budget checks, while quarterly and annual reports support strategic planning and compliance, including VAT reporting requirements in the UAE. Q3. What are the main components of an income statement? Key components include revenue (top line), cost of goods sold (COGS), gross profit, operating expenses, operating profit, finance costs, tax, and net profit. Recognising each component accurately helps business owners and finance teams evaluate profitability and cost control. Q4. How does an income statement differ from a balance sheet? The income statement reports financial performance over a period by showing profits and expenses. In contrast, a balance sheet shows a company’s financial position at a specific point in time by detailing assets, liabilities, and equity. Both are used together to give a full financial picture. Q5. Can an income statement show cash flow details? No. An income statement shows profitability, not the actual cash movements. For cash flow insights, businesses must use a cash flow statement, which tracks the timing of cash inflows and outflows. This distinction is important for UAE businesses to avoid assuming profit equals available cash.

body_text: First set of eight satellites for Globalstar 2-R mission deployed to low Earth orbit on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket, marking the beginning of the commissioning phase TORONTO, ON (August 16, 2026) – MDA Space Ltd. (TSX:MDA; NYSE:MDA), a leading provider of advanced technology and services to the rapidly expanding global space industry, confirms the successful deployment of the initial eight replenishment satellites for Globalstar Inc.’s (NASDAQ:GSAT) existing low Earth orbit (LEO) constellation. Developed and fully integrated and tested in Montréal, the satellites were launched on Saturday, Aug. 15, 2026, at 9:12 p.m. ET aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Space Launch Complex 40 in Cape Canaveral, Florida, and will now undergo a series of in-orbit tests as part of the commissioning phase. This marks a defining moment in MDA Space history, as these LEO satellites are the first to be delivered by MDA Space as a prime contractor for commercial communications constellations. “This program for Globalstar marked a major transformation in our design and high-volume satellite production process, enabling us to accelerate development and manufacturing,” said Mike Greenley, CEO of MDA Space. “With the execution of this constellation nearing completion, and with our new high-volume manufacturing facility now in operation, we are ramping up even further, giving us the capacity to meet customer requirements as market demand increases.” The remaining nine satellites on order are in the final stages of integration at MDA Space. Once fully operational on orbit, they will enable Globalstar to extend the life of its existing constellation, which supports direct-to-device satellite-enabled services on select mobile phones and IoT applications. title: Electronic Design: The Missing Layer in AI Systems Design is Predictable, Scalable Data Movement
summary: The article explores why predictable, scalable data movement is becoming a critical architectural requirement for AI systems as compute complexity and bandwidth demands continue to grow.
body_text: Home » Newsroom » Blog » Electronic Design: The Missing Layer in AI Systems Design is Predictable, Scalable Data Movement Electronic Design: The Missing Layer in AI Systems Design is Predictable, Scalable Data Movement Aug 7, 2026 Andy Nightingale < 1 min read Over the years, AI chip designers have focused on scaling systems, connecting compute, memory, and accelerators. It’s led to an evolution in chiplet architectures. Significant progress has been made in standardizing die-to-die interfaces and advancing packaging, making it easier to assemble more capable systems. These technological advances have received most of the spotlight in this arena. Far less attention has been paid to what happens after everything is connected, specifically how data moves, how it’s prioritized and scheduled, and how reliably it’s delivered under real, multi-tenant AI workloads. It’s not simply a question of bandwidth — it’s a question of deterministic data and control within the fabric. Data-movement predictability ultimately drives performance. When several workloads compete for bandwidth, memory, or interconnect, systems may appear efficient in ideal conditions. However, they quickly lose performance as real load increases. Utilization can become unpredictable, not because of insufficient computing, but because data isn’t delivered when and where it’s needed. When Best Effort Breaks Down The system tries to move data as quickly as possible, but under contention, it often lacks guarantees on latency, bandwidth, or ordering. That model breaks down in AI systems where multiple engines share memory and IO, and where training, inference, and control traffic all have different requirements. title: Premium Dog Food Recalled After Reports of Serious Eye Problems in Pets
summary: A premium fresh dog food company has recalled its products in the UK after receiving dozens of reports that dogs developed symptoms associated with dry eye disease.
